newsitem.title: GERMANY: German business leaders welcome thaw in China-ties.
newsitem.headline: German business leaders welcome thaw in China-ties.

text.p: German business leaders on Wednesday welcomed a thaw in Sino-German ties after Beijing signalled a heated diplomatic row was over, but the opposition Social Democrats accused Bonn of sending a blurred message.

Beijing reinstated an invitation to Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel on Tuesday that it withdrew in June after the German parliament passed a resolution accusing China of trying to erase Tibet's cultural identity.
Germany froze top level contacts in response.

But at a meeting on the sidelines of a United Nations general assembly in New York on Tuesday China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and Kinkel swept aside their differences and pledged to improve bilateral relations.
"We welcome the thaw in relations with China," said Heinrich von Pierer, chairman of the Asia-Pacific Committee of German Business, in a statement.

"A lasting deterioration in the political framework would have had a long-term negative effect on economic ties between Germany and China," said Pierer, who is also chairman of Germany's biggest engineering group Siemens AG.
Bilateral trade of some 27 billion marks ($17.91 billion) last year makes Germany China's biggest European trading partner.
Qichen renewed his invitation to German President Roman Herzog, whose office said he would go there in November, and Kinkel, who plans to visit before that.

While business people like Von Pierer say only more trade can lead to more democracy in China, human rights groups and opposition parties say German leaders have failed to properly address what they call terrible human rights conditions.
Opposition Social Democrat Freimut Duve, who sits on parliament's foreign affairs committee, warned the government not to send confused signals over the Tibet issue.
China often views support for Tibetan interests or Tibet's spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, as implicit support for Tibetan independence.
"We have never supported Tibet's secession, but we want China to restore Tibet's cultural identity and give it as much political autonomy as possible," Duve told German radio.
"The German parliament declared Tibet was wrongfully incorporated into China at the time and I don't think the German government can take a radically different position on this," he said.

Germany's largest industrial group Daimler-Benz, which has several joint ventures and projects in the pipeline in China, also welcomed the Bonn-Beijing detente but said it had carried on business as usual despite the tensions.

"Mercedes-Benz completed a deal to set up a coach joint venture in China at the time when relations were cooler," said a spokeswoman for Mercedes' parent company Daimler-Benz, which recently joined a Western consortium to help build a second subway line in Shanghai.
